title: Supervisory Stress Test Documentation Final 2026 Global Market Shock Component February 2026
summary: The Federal Reserve Board published the final documentation for the 2026 Supervisory Stress Test's Global Market Shock (GMS) component, which applies hypothetical shocks to financial risk factors including equities, currencies, commodities, interest rates, and credit securities under a severely adverse scenario. Firms with aggregate trading assets and liabilities of $50 billion or more, or 10% or more of total consolidated assets, must incorporate these shocks into their stress test projections. Losses from the global market shock are recognized in the first quarter of the scenario horizon, with no changes assumed in subsequent quarters.
key_points: The global market shock component applies instantaneous hypothetical shocks to risk factors including public equity returns, exchange rates, government yields, swap rates, interest rate options, commodity futures, and credit spreads

Firms subject to the GMS include those with aggregate trading assets and liabilities of $50 billion or more, or 10% or more of total consolidated assets (excluding Category IV firms under the tailoring framework)
Losses from the global market shock are recognized in Q1 of the severely adverse scenario's nine-quarter projection horizon, based on the assumption that market dislocations can occur rapidly
The as-of date for position data was October 11, 2024 for the 2025 stress test cycle; firms may use data from their weekly reporting cycle falling within the business week of the as-of date
No revisions were made to this final documentation from the October 2025 proposed version other than typographical fixes
Risk factors are classified into primary, secondary, and remaining categories, with modeling approaches capturing relationships between these factor tiers
why_it_matters: This documentation establishes the methodology by which the Federal Reserve assesses whether large trading firms can absorb losses from severe market dislocations. Understanding the GMS framework is essential for banks and trading desks to anticipate potential capital impacts under stress scenarios, as the shocks directly affect mark-to-market losses on trading and counterparty credit positions.
macro_context: The global market shock component is part of the DFAST (Dodd-Frank Act Supervisory Stress Tests) severely adverse scenario, designed to assess bank capital resilience rather than forecast economic conditions. The macro scenario extends over a nine-quarter projection horizon, with the market shock impact confined to Q1.
market_structure_context: The document details the modeling approach for risk factor relationships, including liquidity horizons for different asset classes, and describes how the Fed calibrates shocks to equity indices, interest rates, credit spreads, and volatility surfaces across key advanced and emerging market economies.
